Anent the first issue, this Department is of the view that, as a general cule, insertion of new items in the annual budget proposed by the local chief executive is not allowed. This finds basis in Article 415 of the Implementing Rules and Regulations and as reiterated in Item 4.5, Chapter III of the Budget Operations Manual for LGUs, cited in the DBM Legal Opinion NO. L-B-2001-6, and which reads: "ART. 415. Budget Authorization. The local sanggunian may not increase the proposed canount iPl the executive budget nor include new items except to provide for statutory and contractual obligations but in no case shall it exceed the total appropriations in the executive buclget. " (Underscoring supplied) "4.5. Limitations on Legislative Action.- The Sanggunian may not increase the proposed amount in the executive budget nor include new items except to provide for statutory and contractual obligations that tnay not have been cortsidered in the preparation of the budget or that the amounts provided may be deficient. In no case, however, shall such additional provision result to the excess of the total appropriations over the proposed in the executive budget. ' Clearly, the aforequoted provision prohibits the inclusion of new itenns not foziild in the executive budget. However, by way of an exception thereto, insettion of new items may be allowed if the purpose thereof is to provide for statutory and contractaai obligations of the local government unit concerned, which were omitted or may have been overlooked in the preparation of the executive budget and provided further that said insertion should not result to an excess of the total appropriations of the execu•ive budget. Anent the second issue, this Department is of the view that the Sangguniang Panlungsod has no authority and power to revise a local development plan duly adopted and approved by the local development councii. Indeed, as you noted in your letter-query, this Department has been consistent with its position on such an issue and still finds no cogent reason to deviate from the same. As has been explained time and again, it is the primary function of the local development council to formulate and initiate the political unit's comprehensive multi-sectoral development plan and public investment program. Thereafter, the plan and/or program should be submitted to Che concerned sanggunian for its appropriate action and approval. However, it has been opined that such submission and approval are only for purposes of enacting the corresponding ordinance so as to comply with the rule that no money should be paid out of the local treasury except in pursuance to appropriations ordinance [Section 305 (a), Local Government Code]. To construe the sanggunian's approval as being inclusive of the authority to revise the projects identified and formulated by the Local Development Council (LDC) would definitely render nugatory the purposes canc\ objectives of the Local Government Code in institutionalizing the LDCs. Thus, if at the sanggunian is not amenable to the LDCs approved projects and programs, the s; sanggunian should instead return the proposal of the LDC with conmnents recommendations and for the LDCs proper consideration [DILG Opinions Nos. 149-t 150-99, 48-02, 84-02, 90-02, 137-03].

R. No. 134213, 20 July 1999] is worthy of note that the situation under the old Local Government Code (BP 337) anymore the same under the new Local Government Code (RA 7160). Under tl Code, the Mayor was made by law as the Presiding Officer of the sanggunian, wh under the new Code, it is now the Vice Mayor. Clearly, there is a legislative inte. really separate the Mayor, as Executive Officer, from the legislative body undet lie new Code. He is expected to perform full time executive functions. Hence, while could be a valid argument under the old set-up that the Presiding Officer (M: should not be included in the number of the sanggunian membership, this i: anymore available in the present set-up under the new Local Government Code to the changes and the legislative intent therefor introduced by the new I Government Code (RA 7160). The total number of members, including the Vice as Presiding Officer, would then serve as the basis in determining whether or noc 2/315 vote required in overriding a veto has been attained. Thus, in a sanggunian with 13 members, including the Vice Mayor, you correct in saying that the exact number of votes required to override your veto is 8. However, it is an obvious fact that there is no such thing as a fractional mc of a sanggunian, such as .56. The membership of the sanggunian wili correspond to a whole number. So, we are now confronted with a choice betw- and 9 members of a sanggunian which is the number required to constitute 2/3's thereof. At this point, it is significant to restate a portion of Section 54 of the I Government Code, which states that "xxx the sanggunian concerned oven-ide the veto of the local chief executive by 2/ 3's vote of all op members xxx". Definitely, if we go by 8 votes, then it is less than 2/3 ne 13-member sanggunian as the 2/3 of the body is mathematically computed as Hence, the logical conclusion in order to comply with the vote of 2/3 would be to tid off 8.6 in such a way that we can come up with a whole number which is cc,rn with the 2/3's votes requirement. Therefore, it is logical to conclude that the 213k of the body should be the affirmative votes of 9 members.
